claims.text: Controlled laser or build-plate preheating during selective laser melting reduces thermal gradients during solidification of high-entropy alloys.
Reduced thermal gradients diminish fabrication-induced defects in selectively laser-melted high-entropy alloys.
Preheating improves the dimensional precision of selectively laser-melted high-entropy-alloy components relative to fabrication without preheating.
Preheating enhances the mechanical integrity of selectively laser-melted high-entropy-alloy components relative to fabrication without preheating.
Preheating produces a more uniform and refined microstructure.
Preheating reduces porosity in the fabricated material.
Preheating lowers residual stresses in the fabricated material.
Preheating reduces the number of crack-initiation sites.
Preheating reduces the temperature differential between the melt pool and surrounding material.
Reducing the melt-pool temperature differential minimizes rapid thermal contraction and residual stresses.
Moderating thermal gradients reduces cracks and porosity.
Moderating thermal gradients enables more accurate layer deposition.
Preheated samples will exhibit lower geometric deviation than non-preheated samples.
Preheated samples will exhibit increased yield strength and ductility relative to non-preheated samples.
The effect of preheating is expected to be greatest for high-entropy alloys processed at high cooling rates.
The effect may diminish when alloy melting characteristics or processing parameters differ significantly from typical conditions.
The intervention may not apply to alloys with substantially lower melting temperatures or under extreme ambient conditions that alter cooling behavior.
Evidence from related materials suggests that reduced thermal gradients improve microstructural uniformity and material properties.
